title: The Minimum Payment Trap: What It Really Costs You
description: The minimum payment trap explained: how card minimums are worked out, what paying only the minimum costs, and how freezing your payment saves years.
keywords: minimum payment trap paying only minimum credit card how minimum payments work credit card payoff calculator
takeaways: Paying only the minimum on $3,000 at 22% takes 15 years and costs about $4,433 in interest.
Keep paying your first minimum as the required minimum falls, and the same debt clears in under five years.
Use the free minimum payment planner to run your own card.
body:
Your credit card statement is full of numbers, and the smallest one gets most of the attention: the minimum payment due. It looks kind. Pay that amount and your account stays in good standing, and nobody charges you a late fee. What the statement does not say in plain words is how long that small payment keeps you in debt, or how much extra money you hand over along the way. That gap between what the minimum feels like and what it actually costs is the credit card minimum payment trap, and it catches people who pay on time, every time. Below you will see how your minimum is worked out, why it shrinks a little every month, and what happens to one balance when you follow the numbers all the way to the end. It finishes with the one change that gets you out: freeze your first minimum payment and keep paying that same amount. ## What the minimum payment really is The minimum payment is the smallest amount your card company requires you to pay each month to keep your account current. Pay it by the due date and you avoid a late fee and a late mark on your credit record. That protection is real. But the minimum was never built to clear your balance on a sensible schedule. It is a "stay out of trouble" amount, not a payoff plan. It keeps the account open and the interest coming in. A low payment on a stubborn balance means a long, expensive stay in debt. Paying the minimum on time is good for your payment history, but the balance itself can still weigh on your score for as long as it sits there. Read next: [How to Build Credit From Scratch](/blog/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch/). ## How your card company works out the minimum Every card sets its minimum its own way, and the exact formula sits in your cardholder agreement. In practice, most issuers use one of two methods: - A flat percentage of your balance, often around 2%. Owe $3,000 and the minimum is about $60. - A smaller percentage of your balance, often 1%, plus that month's interest and any fees added on top. On top of either method, most cards have a floor, a fixed lowest amount, often $25 to $35. Once the percentage works out below the floor, you pay the floor instead, and if you owe less than the floor, you pay the whole balance. These are not made-up patterns. A Consumer Financial Protection Bureau study of card agreements found that the flat percentage method shows up most often at credit unions and smaller banks, while the percentage-plus-interest method is the one most large issuers use. Real agreements in the CFPB's own database blend the two ideas, with wording like "the greater of $30, 4% of your balance, or 1% of your balance plus interest and fees." Your card's version sits in the agreement you accepted when you opened the account. ## Why the minimum shrinks every month Here is the part that quietly works against you. Your minimum is a percentage of what you owe right now. So when your balance falls, your required payment falls with it. A smaller payment sounds like a reward for making progress. In practice, it takes your foot off the pedal at exactly the wrong moment. Interest is charged first. Every payment you make covers that month's interest before a single cent touches the amount you actually borrowed. Early on, interest takes most of the payment. What is left chips away at the balance, slowly. Then, because the balance is a little smaller, next month's minimum is a little smaller too, so the chipping gets slower still. Compare that with an ordinary loan, where the payment stays fixed. With a fixed payment, the interest share shrinks month by month and the share going to your balance grows. The minimum payment runs that pattern in reverse. The longer you stay on it, the weaker your payment gets. That is the whole trap, and it is built into the formula rather than into any mistake you made. ## One balance, followed all the way through Numbers make this easier to see than warnings do. The example below is an illustration with made-up figures, worked out month by month. It assumes no new charges, no fees, and every payment made on time. Real cards charge interest on your average daily balance, so your own figures will differ slightly, but the story comes out the same. Say you owe $3,000 on a card with a 22% APR. That rate is a fair stand-in for a typical card: figures released by the Federal Reserve on October 7, 2026 put the average APR on credit card accounts that were charged interest at 22.36% in August 2026. For the minimum, we will use the common large-issuer formula: 1% of the balance plus that month's interest, with a $25 floor. ### The first month, dollar by dollar Interest for the month comes to $55, because $3,000 times 22% divided by 12 is $55. The minimum payment is 1% of the balance, which is $30, plus the $55 of interest, so you pay $85. Of that $85, the first $55 covers interest. Only $30 reduces what you owe. After a full, on-time payment, your balance is $2,970. Read that again, because it is the heart of the matter. You paid $85 and your debt fell by $30. ### A year of doing everything right Keep paying exactly what the statement asks for. The balance creeps down, and the minimum creeps down with it, from $85 to about $76 by month twelve. After a full year of on-time payments, you have handed over roughly $966. About $625 of it went to interest. Your balance has fallen by about $341, to $2,659. You did nothing wrong. The formula did this. | When | Minimum due that month | Balance still owed | Interest paid so far | |----------------------|------------------------|--------------------|----------------------| | At the start | $85 | $3,000 | $0 | | After 1 year | About $76 | $2,659 | About $625 | | After 3 years | About $60 | $2,089 | About $1,670 | | After 5 years | About $47 | $1,641 | About $2,491 | | Paid off, in year 15 | Final small payment | $0 | About $4,433 | If you stay on the minimum until the end, the $3,000 balance takes 180 months to clear. That is 15 years. The interest adds up to about $4,433, close to one and a half times what you borrowed. In total you repay roughly $7,433 for $3,000 worth of spending. ## The fix: freeze your first minimum payment Now run the same card again with one change. Instead of paying whatever the statement asks for, you keep paying your first minimum, $85, every single month. The required minimum falls away beneath you, $84, then $80, then $70, but your payment does not move. Because your payment stays put while the monthly interest shrinks, more and more of each $85 lands on the balance itself. The payoff speeds up as it goes. The debt is gone in 58 months, which is 4 years and 10 months. Total interest comes to about $1,873. | Plan | Monthly payment | Time to clear the card | Total interest | Total paid | |------------------------|-----------------------------|------------------------|----------------|---------------| | Minimum only | Falls from $85 toward $25 | 15 years | About $4,433 | About $7,433 | | Frozen first minimum | $85 every month | 4 years, 10 months | About $1,873 | About $4,873 | | Frozen, plus $25 more | $110 every month | 3 years, 3 months | About $1,197 | About $4,197 | Same card, same starting payment, no extra money found in month one. Freezing the payment saves about $2,560 in interest and finishes more than ten years earlier. Your balance and rate will differ from this example, and your own numbers are the ones that matter. No sign-up needed. ![The minimum payment planner comparing minimum only, a frozen first minimum and the frozen payment plus extra](/assets/img/posts/minimum-payment-planner-preview-1280x665.webp) ## How to freeze your payment, step by step - Find this month's minimum payment on your statement. If you are just starting to pay the card down, that number becomes your fixed payment. - Change your autopay. Most card apps let you choose between the minimum due, the full balance, or a fixed amount. Pick the fixed amount. If you leave autopay set to the minimum due, it will shrink on its own and quietly undo the plan. - Keep new spending off the card while you pay it down. New charges restart the clock and blur the progress you are making. Read next: [How to Stop Impulse Spending](/blog/how-to-stop-impulse-spending/). - If a bad month hits, drop back to the required minimum for that month rather than missing the payment entirely. You stay current, avoid the late fee, and return to your fixed amount the month after. - When the card reaches zero, send that same payment somewhere useful instead of letting it dissolve into everyday spending. Read next: [How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/). If you carry balances on more than one card, freeze the minimum on each of them so nothing slips backward, then aim every spare dollar at one card at a time. Read next: [Debt Snowball vs Avalanche](/blog/debt-snowball-vs-avalanche/). For a full payoff plan, see [how to pay off credit card debt fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/). ## The warning box already sitting on your statement If your card is from a US issuer, the honest version of this article is already printed on your statement. Under the Credit CARD Act of 2009, issuers have to include a Minimum Payment Warning. It shows how long it would take to clear your current balance paying only the minimum, what that path costs in total, and the monthly payment that would clear the balance in 36 months instead, along with how much the faster path saves you. Most people skip straight past it. Next time your statement arrives, read that box first. Those are your real numbers, for your real balance, and they use the same maths as the example above. Statements in the UK, Canada, and Australia are set out differently, but the same check works with your balance, your APR, and your cardholder agreement. ## When paying only the minimum does make sense There are months when the minimum is the right call. A job gap, a car repair, a week of lost hours. Paying the minimum on time in a month like that protects you from a late fee, a possible penalty rate, and a mark on your credit record. The trap is not using the minimum once. The trap is leaving it as your permanent setting and letting the formula run your payoff for a decade or more. If you cannot cover even the minimum, call the card company before the due date, not after. Ask what hardship options they have, and write down what you agree to. A nonprofit credit counselor can also look at the whole picture with you, often for free. Do not ignore the bill and hope it shrinks on its own. It will not. ## Frequently asked questions ### Does paying only the minimum hurt my credit score? Paying the minimum on time does not hurt your payment history, and on-time payments help it. The problem is the balance that lingers. Owing a large share of your credit limit for a long time can hold your score down, and lenders can see that pattern. The issue is the years spent carrying a high balance. ### How is my minimum payment calculated? Most issuers use either a flat percentage of your balance, often around 2%, or a smaller percentage, often 1%, plus that month's interest and fees. Most cards also set a floor of $25 to $35. Your exact formula is in your cardholder agreement. ### What happens if I pay less than the minimum, or miss it completely? Expect a late fee. Miss by 30 days or more and it can be reported to the credit bureaus, which will hurt your score. Some cards can also apply a higher penalty APR after a missed payment. Paying at least the minimum, on time, keeps all of that away. ### Should I use the 36-month payment from my statement instead? If you can afford it, yes. That figure is worked out to clear your balance in three years, and it will always beat the minimum easily. If it is out of reach, freezing your current minimum is a solid middle step, and you can raise the fixed amount later. ### Can I pay more than the minimum whenever I want? Yes. There is no charge for paying extra, and every extra dollar reduces the balance that next month's interest is charged on. That is why even a small fixed amount above the minimum changes the ending so much. This article is general education about how credit card minimum payments work. It is not personal financial advice. Check your own statement and cardholder agreement for the figures that apply to you, and talk to a qualified adviser or a nonprofit credit counselor if you need help with your specific situation. ## Sources - [Federal Reserve, Consumer Credit (G.19), release dated October 7, 2026.](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/) - [NerdWallet, "How Credit Card Issuers Calculate Minimum Payments," updated September 17, 2025, reporting Consumer Financial Protection Bureau findings on minimum payment formulas.](https://www.nerdwallet.com/credit-cards/learn/credit-card-issuer-minimum-payment) - [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Credit Card Agreement Database, sample cardholder agreement showing a minimum payment formula.](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/a/assets/credit-card-agreements/txt/creditcardagreement_11589.txt)
